videos.title: jay deacon and shayne tabb   modified tennis competition (1080p)

segments.description: Please welcome Shane Tab and Jay Deacon to the Virtual Grand Samp Coaches Conference. Shane is an accomplished tennis coach and educator with multiple accolades, including the Gold Coast Coach Recognition Award in 2018, the Club Recognition Award in 2019, and the Queensland Coaching Excellence Development Award in 2021 and 2024. He's also a Newcombe Coach Excellence finalist for development in 2024. Shane has coached two-time national champion Tori Russell, developed ITF Junior and national level athletes, and mentored multiple NDS and Super 10 level players. Shane co-created the Colourball Circuit for the Gold Coast, established the Bolt Brisbane Finals, and is a valued member of the Tennis Australia Coach Coalition development team and TQ competitive play committee presenting workshops nationwide. Jay is a highly accomplished coach, educator, and former elite athlete with expertise across multiple sports. In tennis, he has coached six national age champions to number one, developed innovative programs like tennis hotshots talent camps, and the red, orange, and green tournament circuits and led 12 consecutive premiership teams. A former number one ranked Australian swimmer and international water polo competitor, Jay has also coached national champions and future Olympians. As a Tennis Australia Coach Developer, University Electra, and ABC Radio Commentator, Jay combines his passion for sport

with education and innovation. Together, they share invaluable insights into creating Colourball Leagues. The premise behind it was that we came across some interesting data that was collected that if a child hasn't played, had a competitive experience in their first year of play, and this is going from four to 12, there's an 80% chance that they're going to drop out of the sport. So we considered that and we knew that this was the case going into our discussions about how we improve things on the Gold Coast. And we started with the theory that in-house or inter-club match play was a big part of something that we could offer as an outcome rather than just having a lesson each week. So the idea then was that they would have lessons, play match play within the club, and then from there we built out a more regional competition which was a red, orange and green ball circuit as also a team's event called Future Stars. Yeah, so we tried to cater for each of the different levels of the pathway. So someone who's being introduced to competition for the first time, someone who's a little bit more experienced and is looking to branch out. So it was a mix of internal and external experiences that helped provide great opportunities for the kids to play. But I guess the best way to describe it is to go back to where we started from. So I was coaching at a private school here on the Gold Coast

and in conversations we wanted to start something up. So we started a red and orange competition back in 2013 and that was between ourselves and one of the other coaches. So it was a real ground-up approach. So we discussed there's a hole, there aren't these playing opportunities. So we looked to see how we could introduce this inter-club experience for our kids in red and orange because they were already starting to play a little bit in green tournaments elsewhere, but we wanted to provide an environment that was safe, friendly and non-threatening. So it was not high stakes either so that their experience was going to be a positive one. From there, the first future stars evolved and that involved a number of clubs on the Gold Coast. We started off with just the four clubs to start with and then it branched out and expanded significantly from there. Then I guess our first meeting was an RA meeting, so a regional assembly meeting here on the Gold Coast. And Shane talked eloquently about what the needs of the kids that we were coaching and came up and we had a conversation afterwards. Yeah, and we put together a blueprint for red and orange and put the ID forward to a few other coaches and ran a pilot and here we are. And the blueprint, initially it was a red and orange stage because as I said, we had the green in some form of fixture or competition format, but it was a period of time.

So from our first conversation, we developed a blueprint about exactly what we wanted and the keys behind it were significant in that in order to meet the developmental readiness of the players and what they were capable of achieving, we had to identify a number of different things that we were trying to achieve from it. This blueprint, we still have documented and took a lot of effort and the depth and breadth of it was considerable. From there, we were able to get off the ground fairly quickly. And in fact, the tournament that you see in this slide is one of the first tournaments at Somerset and the layout we'll get into a little bit later on. Yeah, it was pretty special for the kids and it's about making the children feel special and safe in that environment. And of course, we'll talk about the values later on too, which is more of the outcome. Yeah. So from there, we thought we'd expand on it and try to add a little bit more sort of icing to the cake. And that's when we start the first Gold Coast Regional talent camps and we operated it conjunctly with a dear friend of ours, Anthony Richardson. And Richo jumped on the chance to be involved in the community here on the Gold Coast. And what we did is we included parent education, coach education, some talent identification for the talent side of things. But what did it create a real community in the Gold Coast? Because it was no longer operating in silos.

We were one as one unit. Absolutely. And it also brought the coaches together. The idea was to invite all the coaches to the talent camp to be on court, looking around at all the kids playing and bringing a collaboration together with everybody. Yeah. So I guess from there, we moved into competitive opportunities that would be a representative opportunity for representing the Gold Coast in our respect. And you might want to talk to the Baltic Brisbane. Oh, look, I think it was great the first couple of years to have the circuit working. And I thought it's unfortunate that they didn't have an outcome whereby we could represent our region and play against other regions. So we created the Baltic Brisbane, which was originally three regions. And we had that at the end of the year as our final. And you played for your region, Gold Coast, against Sunshine Coast and Brisbane. So as you can see from the timeline, this is a fairly drawn out process. It didn't happen overnight. And it took a lot of relationship building in between to get people on board. And I guess that's the biggest thing that the legacy from our initial construct is that we have great relationships with the coaches on the Gold Coast. So looking at the Colourball Circuit, so this is the tier that we introduced for the higher competencies. Sitting down, we went through so many things, a number that are up on the screen.

What age groups? And so we might talk to a few of these. So Red, we decided that Aids and Under would be an appropriate age. And the idea being that the competencies, we're looking at overarm, so first and second serve. Orange, we decided to go ten and under for the fact that the child could almost create their own pathway by staying in orange longer instead of coming into green too early, maybe with not the right competencies. And green, we decided after a year of changing to 11 and under, which was highly successful. So it was interesting as well in terms of the competencies we have on the form that a coach has to sign you off, has to tick you off, that you are Red 3 competent. So you must adhere to all those competencies because we don't want to provide someone with a terrible experience when they don't have the same level of play as other players in the group, whether they're going to be beaten significantly each time they step onto the court. So we wanted to create an environment where there was a more representative play of what they were going to experience. So they were going to feel like they were in every single match. And hence, those coach signing off on those competencies was a crucial part of it. We adapted the scoring formats. Yep, so the scoring format for Red was 1 through 15. So first to 15, 14 all wins the next point wins. And then orange, we went fast 4. Very simple, four matches.

We'll go through the format a bit later on. And green, we decided six games. So it really leads up to 12 and unders, which was effectively more than one set. So the key was that we didn't want to overload the families too much. We wanted to put this on the time where the families could come and they would experience it and still have time over the weekend for themselves. So it was keeping the player and the family at the forefront of our concerns. When it came to the court sizes and layouts, the key was that we would adhere to the tennis Australia court sizes. And so we stuck with the 10.97 by 8.23. 5.5 metre court, which it is now with the new nets. And we stuck with the 18.29 for orange and 23.77 for the green size. So we tried to keep it in alignment so that their experiences, no matter where they played, would be just the same. And I think for the Red ball particularly, I think a big win there was having two courts on one court, not having four courts laid up next to each other. So we created a lot of runoff space. And that also enabled a lot of the smaller clubs to take part in it. And that was part of our guiding principles and that we wanted more people involved in it and more clubs involved. So by doubling up on the court space, effectively, you can play a red tournament at a four court, six court venue. So we were able to bring them into the fold just by manipulating or identifying the size of the courts and the number of courts

that would be required. Which also allows the operators to be educated in tournament directing and working off tournament planner. That's right. And they're all implemented in each of the tournaments across the board. We were pretty clear as well for this level as well. We wanted the events separated between the boys and the girls so they had their own event. Yep. And in match play in-house, we created more of a girls versus boys so that a more supported program outside our venue, we were happy to have a gender difference. And also for the Future Stars, being a team event, it was everyone together. So it takes a lot of the focus off my ability to play because I'm part of a team and that was a big part of it. Do you want to talk to the values? Yeah, values is a huge part of it. And you often wonder why we put young children in competition. A lot of people would say that it's probably a bit early, but in my opinion, if you put the values with it and reward those values, we're giving the children an environment of playing competitive tennis, you could say. But also we're actually highlighting the values of how to behave and what's best for them. And on the day, we have rewards that are greater than winning the event. And those rewards are based on best effort and best sportsmanship. And that's an interesting concept because we're putting the person and we're looking at this holistic development of the child.

And the key function of that is we want better people playing our game. And we know that if we instill these values in place, that we're going to have better people at the end of it who are more likely to stay in our sport. And this coming year, so 2025, on the Gold Coast Circuit, there'll be prizes for the four semi-finalists. So no longer playing off first, second or third. So we're identifying you as great players, but the biggest prizes are going to be for the sportsmanship and effort. So I think that sends a clear message and also to do with social media as well. The social media will be publicizing the big photos of the sportsmanship and effort winners. So the financial aspects, I think we started out in the RA with the TIP funding that we have up here of $1,800 to get NETs and so forth. And that first year, it bought $9,000 in for the region. So we actually made money on creating some TIP funding. And now I know that that 30-odd tournament's 10 each color makes up to $45,000 for the region. Yeah, it's an incredible investment that the region made in this unique piece of competition space that has been rewarded and it's value added to the tennis community here on the Gold Coast. And one of the big parts of it that differentiates from regular tournament players having a supervisor or a numpire on court? Yeah, I think from an early stage, it's pretty hard to concentrate and keep score with those children.

And if we can have a supervisor standing next to another child that's maybe scoring on a score sheet, well, there's an educational piece there already. And I think every child at PlayStation that should know how to write a score down and keep score. So we're very big on that supervisor for red and orange-green. We tend to let them run their own matches and we have a supervisor roaming the center. You know, the etiquette is often lost in the competition space. But we think it's an integral part about identifying who the person is and that feeling of self and importance, all those things that go along with it, the way they feel about themselves. It's important to have that link between that and tennis. And so I think this is where our circuit difference differentiates itself from a lot of other things in that we're providing that opportunity for the kids to be a numpire and experience what that's like with the supervision from older players. Yeah, absolutely. And then that takes us sort of the parent-player education. The parent particularly is a it's a child-free, friendly zone. So no parents are on the court. But by having those supervisors and umpires in place, there's no reason for those parents to be on court. That's right. They can sit back and be the spectators that we want them to be. That's exactly right. Be supportive of their children and make sure that they have a good time.

I think part of that parent education piece, too, which I think Jay, you presented on early on, was not just about the behavior of the parent on the court, but it's about the pathway. I think we had an hour with the parents at one stage. We took them off the courts and into a room and and really just worked out while we were playing red and orange and green for the period of time that we do. That's right. And understanding the components of what the pathway looked like for the Hot Shots programs, going from blue, red, orange, and green to the yellow ball. So understanding what the stages were about and what we're trying to teach within each stage. Yeah. Once again, that the etiquette was we covered basically in the parent education and the player education because players have a player information session prior to the start of play where the expectations are going to be designated before the start of play. So I think that's a big part of it so that they understand what they have to do. And particularly for a red competition, when it's new to so many of them, it's their first playing experience outside the club. And then to be thrown into this space, we want to make it comforting and also provide them with an understanding of what they need to be doing on the court when they need to be able to check in, not to be too far away from the tournament desk at time. So understand what the next matches will be, etc.

So and then basically in these spaces, we're preparing for 11, 12 and under tournaments. That's right. You know, and then we get to the draw tights. We make sure that each child has four to five matches a day, which we run a compass draw. And in some cases in the red, we do some round robins with compass draws. Yeah, the scheduling is usually eight o'clock starts finishing around about 12, 30, one o'clock so that the parents can still get a lunch on a Sunday and keeping it a very family environment. Also, just enjoying the Sundays with the family, but just having a taste of what tournament play could look like. That's a big part of it, isn't it? In each of the ones, it will expand for each difference section. The reds will be a bit shorter than the orange, which would be shorter than the greens. Costs are around $35 to play. And like I said, it's four matches, which gives them sort of up to an hour and a half play with a bit of rest in between. And that price factors work pretty good on the Gold Coast. Yeah, administration wise, because it's run through TP, tournament entries, etc. And the scheduling is all done. It's an opportunity for the club owners or club operators to be able to upskill themselves in the administration side of things and the planner and the tournament director. So in terms of the development of the people within the club land, it's a great opportunity if they don't have those skills.

Yeah, that's right. Promotional. Yeah, look, I think it's been incredible to the last couple of years, TQ have taken on board the promotional side of things. And they've done a great job digitally. We now have 10 tournaments in each color, which is promoted throughout the Gold Coast. Also, it has its own website, so people can go on board on Colourball Gold Coast and see how it all works and find out all the information they need. Yeah, I think that the main thing here is that we get the word out that it's there. And now we're getting a lot of players from Brisbane coming in. That's right. And we want to grow this out so that we can build a bigger regional sort of series, which will lead to a better ball for Brisbane, of course. And also lead to more players in our game for longer. Yeah, well, that's what it's all about, isn't it? It's a match play piece that creates that. Yeah, so looking at the breakdown. This is just a brief run through of where we are in terms of the basics of the format. So Red Bull, all trying to run within the space of three hours, which is great. It gives the parents an opportunity to watch their children play number of matches. We try to keep consistent across the board at four and ensure that they're always supervised so that they're learning a few different skills outside and hitting a tennis ball. I think really important though, there's the layout.

You know, the layout of the Red Bull is those two courts on one court. And the orange ball is our orange two court, but it's also Lyon courts with Chawman. So it's a strong line. It's not just Marcus throwing it on the court. That's right. And suddenly they don't move. And there are no discrepancies in terms of, oh, that might have been in, might have been out. It's clearly defined this play area because once they identify that it's my court and someone's gone to a lot of effort to make it look like this, it raises not only the level of play, but the investment of the child back into the sport, which is a huge part of it. And I think also by having this as a match play benchmark, the coaching program becomes better underneath. Absolutely. Absolutely. Because the competition is the driver of our sport, and there are no two ways about it. As that data suggested earlier on would purvey that if they don't experience competition, well, they're not really a tennis player, they're just having a hit. That's right. So why don't we train during the week and play on the weekends like most sports do? That's right. Yeah. So moving on to future stars. So this concept came about we wanted to provide an opportunity without being threatening lower, sort of slightly lower competencies. So it was more an introductory opportunity for kids to play outside their own clubs. And as I said, it started off between two clubs over a day,

and it expanded incredibly out to over 100 competitors, over 12 clubs. And it got so big that we had to separate into North and South divisions because of it. It was just getting too big for what we had. So in terms of growth, what a great opportunity. You might want to talk to the competencies around it. Oh, look, we decided that it would be better to have two under answers. And keep it pretty simple delivery is anywhere on a three meter court for red. Orange, we played only doubles. And now we've just introduced the orange one court as a singles court. So now it's expanded with the orange and green. We only played doubles as well, but we expanded to singles as well. But the idea is that on an orange, you can overarm, serve the temper, first serve an underarm on a second. So it builds out a larger amount of players to enjoy the game. The game of tennis at a competitive level. And develops their competence and confidence in playing the sport. Also, that connection with their other teammates and they introduce themselves to new opponents that they won't have seen before. And that takes a lot of the scary factor away from it. Moving forward, if they decide to go into the competitive space. But if they stay in this space and play socially, it's a great avenue for that as well. So the way it worked was we had eight players per team in red. Four in orange and four in green. And we would come together on one day as six tennis centers

and do a North match and a South match on that same day. And you'd play four or five of those per year. So it was built around one term, but the whole entire clubs would come together on one day and it'd be around Robin of 30 minutes. So playing everybody in that group. And it might be a two minute rotation that they're playing the person in front of them. If they win, they stick up their hands. So very much very similar to the schools concept, whether it's the Tobwood Bridge Cup or the Queensland Primary Schools Cup that we have here. Yeah, and great, a great springboard for the first circuit we're talking about. So if their first external competitive game is this, well, then maybe the next one is the Colourball. Yeah, it's not such a big leap from their internal match play into that external environment. So while it was the first of the external opportunities, it is actually the least confronting. So absolutely. And that's that team environment. Yeah, when we look at competencies, particularly around the red, we're looking at more of the red two competencies. And then also the orange one now that we're looking at. Yeah, so we've expanded the red to five point five minutes now. So the courts are a little bit bigger as well. Yeah, so probably the most important one. And in many cases, it isn't done widely enough. It's the intercom match play, whether it's seen as too hard. I don't know what the case is.

But the reality is that if we have the kids playing, they will improve faster. You made a great comment about you don't have a tennis coaching program. You have a match play program. Yeah, look, I think in the beginning when I first got here, I was doing what I thought I knew best, which was to coach children and activities. And I wondered why we didn't have any competitive play for eight to nine year olds in red and orange. And those eight and nine year olds are playing green ball and not playing it very well. So we decided, look, let's get a red, firstly an orange, then a red internal match by Friday night competition. It turned into four red ball players at the start, which was extremely fearful of. But by putting the values to it and having a lot of support behind it, it built out to 16 players in red and I think 28 in orange, which then created a platform for this regional play and team play. And and also it gave my coaches some some realistic view on what they're working for. That's exactly right. You know, so it's about building a player's competencies to be able to perform in an outcome of playing a match. And the coaches will be all employed on the night and they'd see their own child that they were coaching during the week, play the match that is actually a little bit different than actually doing the activity. Yeah, because we don't actually know how they play if you're not going to watch them.

So this is a great opportunity or the first stepping stone and actually seeing your child play so that then you can work on their development. Well, it's the difference between live ball and non-live ball. That's right. So when they're playing a live ball, it's very different to having a tennis lesson that's not live and the pressure of a match as well. Yeah, so and we again, we put those values heavily around each each player so that they feel like they're achieving the right things. How do you find the interactions between the kids? Do you think it develops that sense of community and a culture within the club? So the format that we we put together was one singles match and then two doubles matches, even in the red space. And the players that would play against each other in singles would be doubles partners and play against the rest of the group. So there was actually a buddy up system. And then if there was eight in a group, it actually became like a buddy up, buddy up system, which for me created a very tribal environment. And then it felt very safe to actually send those children out to the external match play because they were all supporting each other. So ideally we were a football club, but we're a tennis club of players and we created that through that system. Yeah, it's a change in the thinking of this being an individual sport. This is a club sport or a team sport.

And once you start to see that evolve, that's when the biggest changes will take place for your clubs. Once again, the parent education and player education. This is the starting point for having the court supervisors in place that they can help shape the learning that's taking place, but also the learning for the parents because they'll have a greater understanding. I think we have a good success rate externally with our parents because internally we run the same concept. And that is, you know, it's a it's a child playground. It's not for the parents to be on the court guiding the children through it. It's the coaches and the children coming together on the court. And the parents are offside, you know, just enjoying spectating. Yeah. How do you find the competencies? Where do they they fold in for you? As in on the day? Yeah. Yeah. Oh, look, I think the exploration is there's something that really is noticeable. I think if you let them play and they've got the basics of the foundations, what you've been teaching, they start exploring the court differently. Yeah. And that's without any interaction from the coach. It's like, yeah, pretty much self driven. Self guided learning is a big part in the self organization of how they are approaching it and what they're learning and what they're experimenting with as well. They actually drive you forward as a coach, which is kind of cool.

You know, like you have your idea of what you want someone to learn, but then they find something else to learn and they guide you through it. Yeah. So it's a bit of yin and yang. Yeah, absolutely. Yeah. Well, I hope this gives you an idea of where it all started and how it's progressed. We will provide information and the coach development team in each of the states will have the information booklets from the Gold Coast competitions as to the structure, the layout, everything that's needed for delivery. And if you'd like to learn anything more, please reach out to either of us. Absolutely. Thank you, John. Thanks very much. Thank you.
